| [THEORY-170](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-170.md) v2 | Languages differ in what they oblige, not allow | Jakobson (1959), [LIT-786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-786.md), after Boas: every cognitive content can be expressed in any language, but each grammar obliges its speakers to answer certain questions (aspect, number, gender, tense, definiteness). Translating between grammars that ask different questions forces the translator to supply answers the source did not give and to leave unexpressed answers it did, and a chain of translations of an isolated sentence can lose its content, less so the richer the context. Argued from examples, not tested; it concerns cognitive content, not pragmatic force. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-226](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-226.md) | LLM revisions move essays in a shared direction | Abdulhai et al. | [THEORY-1120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1120.md) v3 | COMET tracks pragmatic adequacy at r = 0.81 | Singh et al. (2026), [LIT-1817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1817.md), read in [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md). On 416 outputs (104 items × 4 models), wmt22 COMET correlates with 1–5 pragmatic-adequacy scores at Pearson 0.813, Spearman 0.860; XCOMET ρ 0.792, MetricX ρ 0.788 (Table 3). Four hand-picked outputs scored 0.65–0.86 by COMET and 1–2 by the rater. Each language had one rater, so there is no reliability against which to read 0.81, and the claim that metrics fail "especially for implicature and deixis" rests on per-phenomenon differences of 0.1 or less. | Active |
